title: What Buyers Should Know About Property Boundaries and Surveys
content_html:
Why Property Boundaries Matter More Than Most Buyers Expect

When you buy a home, you're buying more than the structure sitting on the lot — you're buying the land within a specific legal boundary. Most buyers assume the fence line, the hedge, or the edge of the driveway marks where their property ends and the neighbor's begins. Often it does. Sometimes it doesn't. Understanding the difference between an assumed boundary and a legally surveyed one can save a buyer from disputes, costly fixes, or an unpleasant surprise after closing.

This is especially relevant in parts of Temecula Valley, Murrieta, and Menifee where older parcels, hillside lots, agricultural-zoned land, and custom-built homes sometimes have boundary lines that were never precisely marked or that have shifted in practice over decades of fencing, landscaping, and additions.

What a Property Survey Actually Shows

A property survey is a precise measurement of a parcel's legal boundaries, performed by a licensed land surveyor, based on recorded legal descriptions, maps, and physical monuments (markers placed in the ground at corners and along boundary lines). A survey can show:

  • The exact location of boundary lines relative to existing fences, walls, and structures
  • Whether a structure, fence, pool, or other improvement encroaches onto a neighboring parcel — or whether a neighbor's improvement encroaches onto the subject property
  • Easements that cross the property, such as utility or access easements
  • Setback lines required by local zoning, if requested
  • The size and shape of the lot in relation to recorded maps

A survey is a physical, on-the-ground measurement. It is different from a title search, which is a review of recorded documents affecting ownership. Both matter, but they answer different questions.

Survey vs. Title Insurance: Two Different Protections

Buyers sometimes assume that title insurance covers boundary problems. It generally doesn't, at least not comprehensively, unless an enhanced policy or an ALTA survey-based endorsement is purchased. A standard title policy insures against defects in the chain of ownership — things like undisclosed liens, forged documents, or missing heirs. It typically does not guarantee the physical location of boundary lines on the ground unless a current survey was used to underwrite that specific coverage.

That distinction matters because the two issues are genuinely different. A title problem might mean someone else has a competing ownership claim. A boundary problem might mean the fence, driveway, or even part of the house sits in the wrong place relative to the legal lot lines — a physical fact a title search alone won't catch. For a broader look at what title insurance does and doesn't cover, see our guide to title insurance for California homebuyers.

Common Boundary Issues Buyers Encounter

Encroachments

An encroachment occurs when a structure, fence, or landscaping feature from one property extends across the boundary line onto a neighboring property. This is common with older homes where fences were built by estimation rather than survey, or where landscaping gradually crept over a line over many years.

Fence Lines That Don't Match Legal Boundaries

A long-standing fence is not automatically proof of the legal boundary. Fences get built for convenience, not necessarily precision, and a survey can reveal a gap between where a fence sits and where the recorded boundary actually falls.

Easements

An easement grants someone other than the owner a legal right to use a portion of the property for a specific purpose — a utility company's right to access power lines, a shared driveway, or a drainage path, for example. Easements are typically recorded and can affect what an owner is allowed to build or alter on that portion of the lot.

Unclear or Outdated Legal Descriptions

Older parcels, particularly in areas that were historically agricultural or rural before being subdivided, sometimes carry legal descriptions that are harder to reconcile with current fencing and development patterns on the ground.

When Should a Buyer Order a Survey?

A survey isn't automatically part of every purchase transaction. Buyers should consider ordering one when:

  • The property is on a larger lot, a hillside, a rural parcel, or has irregular boundaries
  • There's any visible sign of a fence, structure, or landscaping feature that looks inconsistent with where the lot lines are expected to run
  • The buyer plans future construction, additions, or a pool, and needs to know precisely where setbacks and boundaries fall
  • The seller or listing doesn't have a recent survey on file and the property has changed hands or been subdivided multiple times
  • Neighboring parcels show evidence of disputes, unusual fencing, or shared-use areas like driveways

A buyer's real estate agent, escrow officer, or attorney can help determine whether ordering a survey makes sense for a specific property, and a licensed surveyor can advise on the type of survey needed — a boundary survey, an ALTA/NSPS survey, or a mortgage location survey, which all serve slightly different purposes and carry different levels of detail and cost.

What Happens If a Boundary Problem Is Found

If a survey reveals an encroachment or boundary discrepancy before closing, buyers have options to negotiate: asking the seller to resolve the issue, requesting a boundary line agreement with the neighboring owner, adjusting the purchase price, or in some cases walking away from the transaction if a purchase agreement contingency allows it. This is one more reason a careful review of contingencies in the purchase agreement matters — boundary and survey issues are exactly the kind of discovery a well-drafted contingency is designed to protect against.

If a problem surfaces after closing, resolving it is usually more complicated and may involve negotiation with the neighboring owner, a formal boundary line agreement, or in rare cases, legal action. This is part of why catching boundary issues during the transaction — while there's still room to negotiate or walk away — is far preferable to discovering them afterward.

Practical Steps for Buyers

  • Ask the seller or listing agent whether a prior survey exists for the property, and request a copy if so
  • Walk the property line with a critical eye — compare fences and landscaping features against any available plat map or prior survey
  • Talk to your agent about whether a new survey is warranted given the property's history, lot shape, and location
  • Review any recorded easements that appear in preliminary title reports during escrow
  • Don't assume a fence, hedge, or wall is the legal boundary just because it's been there a long time

Boundary and survey issues are just one piece of a larger due-diligence process during a home purchase. Pairing a careful look at boundaries with a thorough home inspection and a close reading of the contingencies in your purchase agreement gives buyers the clearest possible picture of what they're actually acquiring before the transaction closes.
